Queens Takes the Lead! 2025 Records Reveal Highest Rat-Finding Rate

Borough rankings reveal an interesting story about the pests.

While Brooklyn had the most initial inspection visits in 2025, Queens led the city in the share of initial inspections finding rat activity. More than one in four initial inspection visits in Queens found rat activity! Inspectors recorded findings at 25.6% of its 7,355 initial visits, ahead of the Bronx at 19.6%, Brooklyn at 17.4%, Manhattan at 16.2%, and Staten Island at 6.3%.

Loading borough data…

At a whopping 57,893 initial inspections, Brooklyn accounted for the largest number of initial inspection visits in 2025. Those visits produced 10,058 rat-activity findings, compared with 1,883 in Queens. Do not be fooled by this disparity: Brooklyn had more recorded findings, but Queens had the higher percentage of inspections finding rat activity.

So which borough has the most rats? These records cannot settle that question. They describe inspection visits, and the properties selected for inspection may differ across boroughs. A property can also appear more than once. Queens tops the rate among inspected locations—not a citywide rat census.

December Jump in Queens Raises Questions

Inspection counts add context to a striking turn in the chart.

Queens’ share of initial inspections finding rat activity rose from 19.3% in November to 38.3% in December 2025. December’s figure (the borough’s highest monthly percentage of the year) represented 110 findings across 287 initial inspections.

Yet the month with the highest percentage was not the month with the most findings. In August, Queens recorded 433 findings across 2,400 inspections. Its rate was just 18.0%, but its finding count was nearly four times December’s.

The boroughs did not follow a single calendar. Brooklyn’s highest monthly rate came in September, while Manhattan’s came in October. The Bronx peaked in February.

These differences invite investigation, rather than a simple seasonal explanation. Changes in the number and locations of inspections could influence the pattern. The records alone do not show whether weather, rat behavior, or a shift in inspection coverage drove a monthly rise.

A Hotspot on the Map—but of What?

Overlapping inspection visits reveal where the city looked and what it found.

The blue dots mark initial inspection visits across New York City in 2025. Red dots identify visits that found rat activity, drawn over the blue inspection layer.

Loading map…

Read the colors together. A concentration of red points shows repeated recorded findings in an area, while the blue layer provides context about inspection coverage. Where inspectors make more visits, there are also more opportunities to document rat activity.

Each dot represents a visit, not a rat or necessarily a unique property. Repeat inspections can overlap at the same location, making an area appear darker. The colors do not measure rat populations or calculate a neighborhood’s finding rate.

Empty space requires equal care: it may reflect a lack of inspections, rather than a lack of rats. Records with missing or unusable coordinates are excluded from the map, but remain in the borough and monthly charts.

About the Records

This analysis uses 144,314 initial inspection visits dated January–December 2025 from the NYC DOHMH Rodent Inspection dataset.

Rat-activity findings include “Failed for Rat Activity” and “Failed for Rat Activity and Other Reason.” Percentages are findings divided by initial inspections within each borough or borough-month. The dataset records inspections; it is not a census of rats.

Map outlines: NYC Department of City Planning borough boundaries.
